name: Dark Plumbago Grey
lede: Dark Plumbago Grey darkens [[plumbago-grey]], named for the blue-grey mineral plumbago, and it is unusually common in the work of the painter Albert Marquet.

sections.title: A darkened mineral grey
sections.body:
The name pairs dark with [[plumbago-grey]]. Plumbago is an old name for graphite and for the blue-flowered shrub of the same name, both lending their cool grey-blue to the color word [1]. Ridgway charted this darker tone in his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, plate L, hue 61′′′′, and the ISCC-NBS *Dictionary of Color Names* carried it forward in 1955 as block 228 [1].

Its nearest measured neighbors are [[purple-slate]] and [[lavender-purple]], each about 3.3 units away and almost the same color; [[madder-blue]] is a little more vivid, and [[crayon-blue]] sits further out at 5.1 units, also close to the same color [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A match for this color covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 250 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.1 per cent, as photographed [3]. It is strongest in the work of Albert Marquet, 3 of his 16 paintings, nearly 17.8 times the archive's overall rate, and in Theodor Philipsen's, 5 of 29 [3]. The earliest dated match, Gentile da Fabriano's *Adoration of the Three Kings*, dates to 1423, a floor on the color's age in painting rather than a claim of its first appearance [3]. As photographed: these are computed color matches on museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment test [3].
